title: Which three different fractional units add up to one?
description: One circle must be filled with three different fractional units. We start from three thirds, let one third grow, and find the last piece by taking away in sixths.
teaching_notes: One idea: grow the units step by step, then find the last piece by taking away in one common unit. Watch for students who guess the next unit from a pattern, or who repeat a unit.

video_script.why: The child reasons about which fractional units are bigger or smaller, and uses a common unit to check that three units fill one whole exactly.
video_script.substitution: One circle, as in the book's figure, filled with pieces of different fractional units, checked for no gap and no spill.
video_script.anchor: one circle to be filled with three pieces, each a different fractional unit, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: One half, one third and one sixth add up to one whole

final_answer.spoken: one half, one third and one sixth

video_script.fraction_reading: one third, one half, one fourth, two fourths, one sixth, three sixths, two sixths, five sixths, six sixths
never_show: the three units written together as a sum equal to 1 before the answer beat
maths_rules: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1, but the three units are the same
to make the units different, one 1/3 must grow; the only fractional unit bigger than 1/3 is 1/2
with 1/2 placed, the rest must make 1/2; 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 repeats a unit
one 1/4 must grow; the only fractional unit bigger than 1/4 and different from 1/2 is 1/3
this is the only solution, up to changing the order
video_script.design: One idea: grow the units step by step until three different units fill the whole, then take away in sixths for the last piece. The circle stays on the board from start to end.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a puzzle from your book about adding fractional units.
<bookmark mark='circle'/>One circle is the whole, and it must be filled with three pieces.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>All three pieces must be different fractional units. Which three make one whole?

beats.on_screen: the circle holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three small circles: cut into 2 equal parts, 3 equal parts, 4 equal parts; every part of each circle is shaded and labelled 1/2, 1/3, 1/4

marks.same: three small circles appear beside the big circle
marks.fill: every part of each small circle is shaded one by one and each circle fills up
marks.ask: a question mark appears over the big circle with the note all different

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>First look at sums that use the same unit again and again.
<bookmark mark='fill'/>Two halves fill a circle. Three thirds fill a circle. Four fourths fill a circle.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Here all three pieces must be different, and that is the puzzle.

beats.on_screen: Given: one whole circle, and three pieces that are all different fractional units

marks.given: the whole circle and the rule all different are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, one whole circle, and three pieces that are all different fractional units.

beats.on_screen: To find: the three fractional units that add up to 1

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the three fractional units that add up to one.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1; one 1/3 must grow; the only fractional unit bigger than 1/3 is 1/2

marks.three: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1 is written and the three thirds fill the circle
marks.same: the circle is shown as a whole broken into equal pieces
marks.grow: one 1/3 piece glows and an arrow shows it growing
marks.half: the 1/3 piece is swapped for a 1/2 piece

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step one, start with three thirds, which fill the circle. The pieces are all the same, though.
<bookmark mark='same'/>A whole broken into equal pieces is the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='grow'/>To make the pieces different, one third must grow.
<bookmark mark='half'/>The only fractional unit bigger than one third is one half, so one half must be a piece.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: with 1/2 placed, the rest must make 1/2; 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 repeats a unit; one 1/4 must grow; the only unit bigger than 1/4 and not 1/2 is 1/3

marks.rest: the 1/2 piece is placed and the other half of the circle glows
marks.fourths: 1/4 + 1/4 is written and a note says same unit again
marks.grow: one 1/4 piece glows and an arrow shows it growing
marks.third: the 1/4 piece is swapped for a 1/3 piece

narration: <bookmark mark='rest'/>Step two, with one half placed, the other two pieces must make one half.
<bookmark mark='fourths'/>Two fourths make one half, but they repeat the same unit.
<bookmark mark='grow'/>To make them different, one fourth must grow.
<bookmark mark='third'/>The only fractional unit bigger than one fourth, apart from one half, is one third.

marks.sum: 1/2 + 1/3 becomes 3/6 + 2/6 with the circle cut into 6 equal parts
marks.five: 5/6 is written and 5 parts of the circle are shaded
marks.left: 6/6 − 5/6 = 1/6 is written and the 1 empty part glows

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step three, find the last piece. In sixths, one half and one third are three sixths and two sixths.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Together they make five sixths.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The whole is six sixths, and six sixths take away five sixths leaves one sixth.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1; no gap and no spill

marks.back: the three pieces slide into the circle
marks.add: 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1 is written and the circle is full with no gap and no spill

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check by putting the answer back in the question.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Three sixths, two sixths and one sixth add up to six sixths. That fills the circle with no gap and no spill.

marks.only: a note says only one solution, up to changing the order

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>One half, one third and one sixth add up to one whole.
<bookmark mark='only'/>This is the only solution, apart from changing the order.
